extracted.intended_audience: PR and communications professionals (particularly healthcare PR practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on applying Dr Robert Cialdini’s six principles of persuasion to plan and run PR and marketing campaigns, with concrete examples from healthcare practice. Aims to help communicators design activity that increases influence, trust and campaign uptake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence shows that people are more likely to follow the behaviour of others who they perceive as similar to them, especially in situations when they are unsure of how to act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use messages that communicate high participation or support (e.g. signs stating '95% of patients at this practice turn up to appointments'). Examples: Cialdini’s NHS work reduced DNAs by 31.4% using social-proof signage; Evergreen PR’s Tinnitus Manifesto leveraged social proof to generate 140,000 petition signatures and high-tier media attention. Apply by highlighting peer behaviour, endorsements from similar people/groups, and momentum to make audiences follow suit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Cialdini argues that people follow the lead of credible, knowledgeable experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build and communicate credibility through visibility, evidence of effectiveness and thought leadership that adds genuine value. Practical tactics include leveraging trusted professions (doctors, scientists, nurses), showcasing expertise and research, and increasing an organisation’s visible authority — especially important in healthcare PR to increase trust and achieve organisational priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commitment and consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: People try to be consistent with their past decisions, statements and behaviours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design processes and activity that secure small, early commitments which lead to larger commitments (e.g. asking patients to verbally repeat appointment details and fill in appointment cards). Apply audience research to understand existing habits and preferences, and adopt a full-funnel focus to create incremental commitments that set people on a path to greater engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocity
rubrics_metrics.description: People are more likely to give back to others when they have received something first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reciprocity through free trials, downloads, special offers or relationship-focused value to encourage return behaviour. Example: The 'Coca Cola experiment' where giving someone a drink increased ticket purchases; in PR, create distinctive value for high-priority stakeholders who may then support your campaign. Consider both transactional and relational forms of reciprocity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scarcity
rubrics_metrics.description: People want things more when those things are in short supply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ scarcity cues such as demonstrating high demand (empty shelves), restricted supply (limited edition) or time-based scarcity (available until). PR examples: offer a journalist an exclusive if they commit within a timeframe, or run a launch where the first 100 sign-ups get free access. Use scarcity ethically and clearly to increase perceived value and urgency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liking
rubrics_metrics.description: People are more influenced by people they like; we are more likely to like people who are similar to us, familiar to us and who cooperate with us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage similarity, familiarity and cooperation to increase influence: use real human case study stories, well-chosen celebrities/influencers familiar to the target audience, and build cooperative, trusted relationships with stakeholders. While not an exact science, these tactics align with behavioural insights to improve campaign outcomes.
